title: The Best Tailgating Vehicles of 2026
summary: When people go to a football game, people tailgate. We’ve chosen nine vehicles that will make your parking-lot party even better.
body_markdown:
When a slight chill first permeates through the air in the fall season, for millions of Americans it means one thing: Football season. Across the country, people devote time, effort, and a larger-than-average snack budget every Sunday to hang out and watch their favorite team face off against another. But sitting at home or at the bar is only so fun for some—why not bring the party to the big game?


Whether you’re inclined to pull up and party down at a local high school game, college game, or an NFL game, football fans across the country will fill their cars with barbecue grilles, coolers, folding chairs, pop-up tents, and cornhole sets, to recreate a backyard party in the parking lot of the local football stadium. We’re talking about the quest to put on one heck of a tailgate party.


When it comes to a great tailgate, the automotive aspect is almost as important as the hot dogs and burgers. You don’t necessarily need a crew-cab pickup truck, but the best tailgate vehicles need to provide plenty of cargo space, they should keep electronic appliances powered and charged, and most importantly, there should never be any question about their ability to make it to the stadium.

## 1. Honda Ridgeline


**CarGurus expert rating:** 7.8 out of 10

Great handling Outdated technology

The Honda Ridgeline shook up the pickup-truck marketplace when it made its debut in the 2006 model year, but it solidified itself as one of our favorite—albeit quirky—pickups after it staged a comeback in the 2017 model year. With a unibody architecture similar to the Honda Pilot’s, the Ridgeline is supremely comfortable, considering its hauling capabilities.


Payload capacity measures a respectable 1,583 pounds in Sport trim and the bed is large enough to carry all your tailgating equipment. A versatile, dual-direction multifunction tailgate makes accessing all that stuff easy, too. It can be lowered like a regular truck’s tailgate, or it can swing out like a car door—think of it like the truck version of the first-generation Honda CR-V. You don’t need to rely on the car’s regular sound system, either; Honda sells the Ridgeline with available in-bed stereo speakers. And, once the tailgate is out of the way, you can easily access the Ridgeline’s under-floor storage compartment. This handy bin is watertight until you pull the drain plug, meaning it’s ideal for use as a cooler, keeping drinks and other items nice and cold.


**The CarGurus Verdict:** *"It doesn’t offer the towing capacity or off-road capability of more traditional trucks, but the Ridgeline is much easier to live with." -Stephen Edelstein*

For tailgating, the 2025 Land Rover Range Rover brings the kind of comfort and curb appeal that makes the parking lot feel like a premium lounge. Its regal luxury vibe works well when you’re hosting friends before kickoff, and the stylish design helps it feel special even in a sea of big SUVs. Tailgates don’t always happen on perfect pavement, and the Range Rover’s standard all-wheel drive is a real advantage when grass fields, muddy lots, or snow-slicked stadium roads are part of the plan. The tradeoff is day-to-day usability around the infotainment and controls: the tech can be unintuitive when you’re juggling food, drinks, and a crowded cabin, and the overall value equation isn’t great compared with less expensive luxury SUVs. Still, if your tailgating routine includes long drives, unpredictable conditions, and a preference for high-end comfort, the Range Rover fits that lifestyle well.

For tailgating, the Ram 1500 plays to the strengths that make full-size pickups such popular game-day vehicles: lots of flexible space, a comfortable place to hang out between plays, and the ability to bring along bigger coolers, grills, and canopy gear without playing trunk-Tetris. For 2026, Ram leans into what many truck shoppers still want most by bringing the available Hemi V8 back to the lineup, giving fans of that classic V8 feel another reason to park a 1500 at the stadium lot.


The lineup’s mix of powertrains and its range of trims matters here, because tailgating isn’t one-size-fits-all: you can prioritize a more upscale cabin for longer drives and postgame traffic, or choose a more rugged, off-road-ready style if your “parking spot” is a grassy field. Just note that some advanced safety features may require stepping up in trim or options, and there isn’t a bare-bones two-door work-truck configuration—so if you’re shopping specifically for the simplest, cheapest tailgate-and-haul setup, you’ll be looking at crew-cab style models instead.

The tech is straightforward, which matters when you’re juggling passengers, parking-lot traffic, and a pregame playlist, and the Ioniq 5’s styling gives it a fun, modern vibe that suits a weekend hangout.


It also brings extra-fast charging into the equation, a practical advantage when your game-day plan includes a last-minute top-off en route or a quick recharge between stops. For tailgating, the Pacifica’s biggest advantage is how quickly it can switch roles from people-mover to gear-hauler. Chrysler’s Stow ’n Go seating is a real-world win when you’re loading coolers, folding chairs, a grill, and team flags—because you can create a big, flat cargo area without wrestling heavy seats out of the garage. And with genuinely usable third-row legroom, it’s easy to bring the whole crew to the game without turning the last row into a penalty box.


A light refresh gives the Pacifica a new face, but it doesn’t change the core experience: strong, confidence-inspiring V6 power for highway merges and postgame traffic, paired with a few drawbacks that matter on long drives to away games. Real-world fuel economy can come up short versus EPA numbers, and the tech interface can feel dated next to newer rivals—though for many tailgaters, the priority is still space, flexibility, and comfort over the latest screens.

For tailgating, the Ioniq 9’s big advantage is simple: room. ## What Makes CarGurus Best Cars Guides Different?


Most car-shopping websites publish lists of the best cars across a variety of categories, with recommendations generally driven by editorial expertise. Here's what makes ours different: In addition to the insights and verdicts of our team of car-testing experts, our best cars guides take into account other factors that we know matter to buyers-real owner experiences and current market value.


Our expert reviewers are among this country's most trusted automotive journalists, also writing for publications including US News and World Report, Edmunds, Digital Trends, J.D. Power, and Car & Driver. They put each car through real-world testing and create detailed reviews of performance in a range of categories, from practicality and driving manners to cost-effectiveness and safety.


We also analyze hundreds of thousands of used car listings on CarGurus.com to track which models consistently offer the highest percentage of best deals relative to how many are listed for sale. Then we factor in reviews from owners-people who actually live with these cars every day. Our proprietary Best Cars algorithm then creates a final **Overall CarGurus rating** combining expert scores, user reviews, and the percentage of listings that have earned the Good or Great Deal rating. This multi-pronged approach reveals not just which cars excel on paper, but which ones deliver satisfaction and value when you're ready to buy.
